title: Apple Music will require Made With AI labels on generated tracks later this year
subtitle: Labels and artists must self-declare AI involvement across tracks, compositions, artwork, and videos — a mandatory disclosure regime built on declaration, not detection.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Apple Music told industry partners in an email on August 20 that it will require a Made With AI label on any track where AI played a substantial role in the creation. The label will cover tracks, compositions, artwork, and music videos, and the requirement will roll out later this year. Apple's system relies on labels and artists to declare AI involvement — there is no automated detection at ingest. Apple Music VP Oliver Schusser said in April that the company has built in-house tools that can identify which AI model produced a given track, but Apple is not using those tools to police the mandate.

The scale problem behind the announcement is real. Apple Music has said that more than a third of tracks uploaded to the service are 100 percent AI-generated, while listening on those tracks remains below 0.5 percent. The disclosure requirement is Apple's answer to a growing catalog of material no listener is asking for. It also draws a distinction the industry has been dodging: a Made With AI label describes AI involvement — it does not settle whether the training data was licensed or whether performers were credited. Those questions run through the Suno and Udio copyright cases, and through the German GEMA v. Suno verdict earlier this month.

The move puts Apple in front of Spotify on labeling and roughly in line with the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency obligations that took effect August 2. YouTube began automatic AI labeling of uploads last year. Streaming disclosure is quickly becoming the norm rather than the exception, though the enforcement mechanisms — declaration versus detection versus watermarking — are still fragmented across platforms.

For learners: keep the two questions separate when you read announcements like this one. One question is whether AI was used to make the thing. Another is whether the person who made it had the right to. A disclosure label answers the first and does not touch the second, and the news coverage often blurs them.
